title: Check yourself: the legacy date classes

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: An order service keeps `private static final SimpleDateFormat DAY = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd")` and uses it in its request handler to parse the due dates clients send. A load test runs 16 clients at once and checks every parsed date against the text that was sent. What does it find?

options.text: Some parses throw, and the rest come back right, since a disturbed parse fails instead of returning a value
options.says: most corrupted parses return a wrong date silently; the exceptions are the minority, and they are NumberFormatException and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

options.text: No parse goes wrong, since each parse copies the Calendar and DecimalFormat it needs before it uses them
options.says: the Calendar and DecimalFormat are instance fields the formatter uses as scratch space, shared by every thread

options.text: Some parses come back wrong, and nothing is logged, since all threads share one Calendar and DecimalFormat
options.says: the shared formatter's Calendar and DecimalFormat are overwritten by concurrent parses, and most failures return a wrong date silently

options.text: No parse goes wrong, since parse and format synchronize on the formatter's Calendar while they use it
options.says: SimpleDateFormat is not synchronized; its javadoc asks for one instance per thread

origin.section: One SimpleDateFormat Shared by Threads Returns Wrong Dates

questions.stem: Two servers log the same row's `java.util.Date` with `log.info("due " + due)`. One prints `Tue Jun 03 01:15:00 CEST 2025`, the other `Mon Jun 02 19:15:00 EDT 2025`. Operations asks which server holds a wrong value. What do you answer?

options.text: Neither: both hold the same calendar fields, and each JVM prints them with its own default UTC offset
options.says: a Date holds no calendar fields, only milliseconds; the two lines even show different days

options.text: Neither: both hold the same millisecond count, and each JVM prints it in its own default time zone
options.says: a Date is only milliseconds since the epoch; toString() uses the printing JVM's default zone

options.text: One of them: a Date holds the time zone ID it was created in, and one server used a wrong ID
options.says: a Date stores no zone; the zone printed is the one of the JVM that prints it

options.text: One of them: a Date holds the calendar fields it was created with, and one server shifted them
options.says: a Date stores no calendar fields; the same value prints as different days in different zones

origin.section: A Date Has No Zone; toString() Uses the JVM's Default

questions.stem: `final class Invoice { private final Date dueDate; Invoice(Date d) { dueDate = d; } Date getDueDate() { return dueDate; } }`. A reminder job runs `Date r = invoice.getDueDate(); r.setTime(r.getTime() - 3 * DAY_MS);` to work out when to send a reminder. What does `invoice.getDueDate()` return afterwards?

options.text: The original date, since a final field keeps the Date it refers to from changing
options.says: final fixes the reference, not the contents of the Date

options.text: Three days earlier, since setTime made the invoice's field refer to a new Date
options.says: setTime changes the object in place; a final field can't be made to point anywhere else

options.text: Three days earlier, since the job changed the Date that the field refers to
options.says: the getter handed out the invoice's own Date, and setTime changes that object; final only fixes which object the field points to

options.text: The original date, since a getter gives the caller its own copy of the field
options.says: this getter returns the field itself; Java copies nothing unless the code does

origin.section: A Date Is a Mutable Moment, So Anyone Holding It Can Move It

questions.stem: A nightly job counts distinct payment days by adding `new java.sql.Date(rs.getTimestamp("paid_at").getTime())` for every payment to a `HashSet`. Two payments were made at 09:10 and 16:40 on one day, and both values print as `2025-05-06`. How many entries does that day contribute?

options.text: One, since the constructor drops the time and equals compares the dates
options.says: the constructor keeps the time of day, and equals compares getTime(); only toString() shows just the day

options.text: Two, since equals compares object identity and the job built two separate objects
options.says: equals compares the millisecond values, not identity; equal milliseconds would give one entry

options.text: One, since toString drops the time and equals compares the printed days
options.says: equals compares getTime(), not the printed day; two values that print the same day differ when their milliseconds differ

options.text: Two, since the constructor keeps the time and equals compares the milliseconds
options.says: java.sql.Date's constructor keeps the full millisecond value, and equals compares getTime()

origin.section: java.sql.Date Is a java.util.Date That Breaks Its Parent's Contract

concepts: A final Date field fixes which object the field refers to, not the moment inside it, and a getter that returns the field hands out that object.
A SimpleDateFormat shared by threads returns wrong dates, most of them without any exception, because it parses into a Calendar of its own; DateTimeFormatter is safe to share.
The java.sql.Date(long) constructor keeps the time of day, so two values that print the same day are not equal.
